nameStory: The razorbill gets its striking name from its distinctive bill, which is flattened sideways like an old-fashioned straight razor blade. This sharp, narrow profile makes it instantly recognizable among seabirds. Early sailors and fishermen who encountered these birds along rocky coasts were struck by this knife-like bill shape.
description: The razorbill is a chunky, penguin-like seabird that's equally at home diving underwater or flying through ocean spray. These black and white birds are about the size of a small duck, with a distinctive flattened bill that looks like it was squeezed in a vise. They're part of the auk family, which includes puffins and murres, and they spend most of their lives at sea. Razorbills are excellent divers, using their wings to 'fly' underwater while hunting for fish.

idTips.label: Razor-flat bill
idTips.description: The bill is dramatically flattened from side to side, creating a thin, knife-like profile that's unmistakable. In breeding season, it develops a distinctive white line across it, making it look even more striking.

idTips.label: Tuxedo coloring
idTips.description: Sharp contrast between jet-black upperparts and bright white belly and chest, creating a formal 'tuxedo' appearance. The white is so bright it almost glows against dark ocean waters.

idTips.label: Chunky swimming posture
idTips.description: Sits low in the water with a compact, rounded body shape. Unlike gulls, it appears heavy and substantial, riding the waves rather than floating lightly on top.

idTips.label: Fast, whirring flight
idTips.description: Flies with rapid, constant wingbeats that create a distinctive whirring sound. Wings appear short relative to body size, and flight looks almost frantic compared to gulls' graceful soaring.

idTips.label: White wing stripe
idTips.description: In flight, shows a thin white line along the trailing edge of each dark wing. This stripe is visible both from above and below, creating a subtle but consistent field mark.

habitat: Along New England's rocky coastlines, especially around offshore islands and steep coastal cliffs where they nest in crevices. Look for them in ocean waters near places like the Maine coast, around Machias Seal Island, or off Cape Ann. They prefer areas with cold, nutrient-rich waters that support abundant small fish like herring and sardines.

seasonality.spring: Razorbills return to coastal breeding colonies in May and June, when their bills develop the distinctive white stripe. This is the best time to see them close to shore as they court and establish nesting territories in cliff crevices.
seasonality.summer: Adults are busy feeding chicks and can be seen making frequent trips between feeding areas and nesting cliffs. Young birds fledge in late summer, creating brief opportunities to spot family groups near shore.
seasonality.fall: Most razorbills head farther out to sea or migrate south, becoming much harder to spot from shore. Occasional individuals may still be seen from headlands during migration.
seasonality.winter: Razorbills are generally far offshore in winter waters, though some may be spotted from ferries or during organized seabird watching trips. Their bills lose the white stripe during non-breeding season.

funFact: Razorbills are the closest living relatives of the extinct great auk, a flightless 'penguin of the north' that was hunted to extinction in 1844—making every razorbill sighting a glimpse at evolutionary history that almost vanished forever.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with murres, which share the black and white 'tuxedo' look, but murres have pointed, dagger-like bills while razorbills have that unmistakable flattened 'razor' bill. Remember: 'Razor-bill' = flat like a blade, murre bill = sharp like a needle.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'auks,' razorbills are not related to the great auk that once lived in the same waters—they're from different genera entirely, though both belong to the auk family. The great auk was flightless and penguin-sized, while razorbills are excellent fliers about the size of a duck.
compareHints: Razorbills are the only species in their genus Alca, making them unique among New England seabirds. Compared to their closest family relatives, puffins have colorful beaks and rounder heads, while murres have longer, thinner bills and more slender necks. The razorbill's flattened bill and stockier build make it the 'bulldozer' of the auk family.
